utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. And Mr. Borovic had some more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that at a certain point at the hangar there were some senior officers there. You also stated they wore olive-drab uniforms, and the third thing you said was that you were under the impression that they were sent there to assist from a superior or by a superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you say these people were officers, did they have any rank, and whether any of them was at the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember their ranks, but some of them did have some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard of Colonel Bogdan Vojinovic [as interpreted]? A correction for the transcript, Bogdan Vujovic [as interpreted]. Again, Bogdan Vujic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know of a Bogdan Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is logical that I ask you: When did you find out who that person is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him subsequently when the testimonies began -- beginning from 2001 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us what is it that you heard, who that officer was, and how come you heard of him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that he came with a group of officers to assist, to lend a hand to the Operations Group South on behalf of the SSNO during the critical period. But personally he had nothing to do with what was taking place at Ovcara between the 18th and the 20th November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about his officers, did they have anything to do with the events at Ovcara, beginning with the 18th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, I presume that one of the officers who were middle-aged and who were at the hangar on the 20th of November, 1991, that there were some who may have been from his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who their superior was at the SSNO, being the federal secretariat for national defence, to make it clear for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is of any relevance for my testimony, but I was told they were from the security administration headed at the time by General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether such a question was put to you during your testimony, but did you hear whether Aleksandar Vasiljevic was at Ovcara or in the area of Vukovar during the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't see him in Vukovar, and I haven't heard of his present there. But subsequently I read somewhere that at a certain point he was there, but I don't believe it is of relevance to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These officers who were somewhat older, so to say, were they also compiling a list in the hangar? I believe you mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the detainees were approaching the table to be identified, they went after the detainees asking them questions, and making notes in their notebooks. That's what I could see. They wanted to know who those people were and from where did they come. Therefore, I distinguished them as a separate group because they seemed to put similar questions and I thought they were security officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On that day did Dragi Vukosavljevic come to the hangar on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having met him there, but I also cannot deny him being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard of Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Subsequently. And again, irrelevant to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to the front line, when you were sent to go to the front line, you said you went to Sid. Were you received by anyone there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came the entire group of officers from the centre of military educational institutions, we came to Sid and we were received by the commander or the Chief of Staff, I can't recall precisely, of the 1st Guards Motorised Division. He told us that we are to be sent to a unit which refused to carry out its task and that they were simply disbanded, the unit fell apart literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've described your presence in the hangar in detail on both occasions, and you explained what you did there. You also explained what (redacted) soldiers were doing, what the 80th Kragujevac Brigade was doing, what the military policemen were doing. My question will be quite specific. 6 During the time before the last (redacted) soldiers withdrew from the hangar, were they -- were any groups taken away to be executed? Then whether anyone was executed either inside or just in front of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information. Those soldiers that were lent to Vojnovic (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm attorney Novak Lukic on behalf of Veselin Sljivancanin's defence. I will be putting questions to you which will mostly pertain to facts. That's what I'm mostly interested in. We will not delve into many theoretical questions. Thus we will need to be in private session for quite a large portion of time. However, initially, we can start off with some general questions to which I hope to receive relevant answers from you. In your view, or perhaps you know the accurate figure in view of the information you might have had, how far is Ovcara from Negoslavci, the Ovcara compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps ever in the Vukovar barracks during that period of time? I am interested in knowing how far specifically the barracks is from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I visited the Vukovar barracks only after the 18th or rather the 20th -- no, I'm sorry, the 22nd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're in open session, so you needn't go into such details. Is there any populated settlement between Negoslavci and Ovcara, or are these mostly uninhabited, rural areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are mostly uninhabited areas, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time the decision of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, which was in existence at the time prescribed that reservists could stay at the front for up to 45 days. Were you aware of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief you said that it was relatively hard to implement mobilisation during that period what can you tell us about what you knew to make you conclude that mobilisations at that time were rather unsuccessful? Shall we go into private session? Yes, let's go into private session. I was hoping to get a general answer, but if you wish we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I know much about such general issues but there are some things that I was aware of. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we are now back in open session. I understand you want to put some submissions to me in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would seek the Court's guidance in relation to one matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will arrange now for the witness to leave the courtroom for a temporary time. It will be necessary for the shutters to close and then open again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then I would ask to go into private session, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind leaving the court with the court officer now, it should not be long, I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore, the submissions you want to put, are they able to be heard in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Regrettably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One second, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do, my lord, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, may I just clarify one or two matters, please. On one occasion you were asked by Mr. Vasic on behalf of Mr. Mrksic about various reports, intelligence reports and security information that you should or should not receive when you are at (redacted). If we deal with the period when (redacted), to whom did you receive the intelligence reports and security information from? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make application that we go into private session, please? For the remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how long the submission of Ms. Tuma will take, but I just wanted to indicate that we have a brief housekeeping matter to raise concerning the proceedings. So I just wanted to have -- to tell you this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tuma, we have 12 minutes remaining, of which sometime is needed for housekeeping. Does this mean that your last starring performance is going to be cut short?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I don't mind that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you think you can leave it in the hands of others?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Absolutely. It depends actually on the Defence, because the Defence has concerning this -- it's one document that the next witness is -- had been recalled by the Defence. So it's more or less up to the Defence, because I don't know how long time they would need in order to further cross-examine that witness. For my part, there is not so many questions, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, casting your eye around your colleagues, can you say whether there will be any questions? Because if there will, I think it's inevitable that we will have to go over to next week. Mr. Vasic is being volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will take up this task to reply to this question. As for my cross-examination of the next witness, I think it will take up to five minutes. I have just very few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we allow five minutes there, five minutes to bring the witness in, and then Ms. Tuma, we're already out of time for the other matters that need to be raised because we're now down to 10 minutes. So, I'm sorry, Ms. Tuma, my concern is though for the witness. It will appear that she will need to remain here over a long weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. She can remain here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She can, can she?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah. I've asked her and she is available and she can stand -- take the stand on Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would convey to her our apologises for the delay, but it's just not possible to fit in her evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I will Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second issue is a matter of the 92 bis and it also seems to me to be something that is likely, even if there was no opposition, to take longer than the nine and a half minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Perhaps ten minutes. I would say it is better to take that on Tuesday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Moore, in time, will come to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I do hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we, before you are asked to sit, indicate to you our good wishes for your new step in your legal career, and we hope that you find it rewarding.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour. I really appreciate that you mention this, and I will hopefully do it with honour, as it is my intent to do that. So I will start at the war crimes chamber in Sarajevo on the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So -- but I was whispering -- whispering here that I will back here on Tuesday. A final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, and than you for that. And we will now turn to housekeeping. Is it Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will now speak on behalf of the Defence of Veselin Sljivancanin, but let me say once again that I do not have instructions from my client in relation to this, to the contrary, his instructions are opposite of what I want to say, but I think that I'm speaking in the interest of his defence. This has to do with the decision to hold all-day trials, which is supposed to take place in May, both in the morning and in the afternoon. Let me state to you clearly that Mr. Sljivancanin is in -- supports this all-day schedule. I have, however, to inform you of something else, and I hope that Mr. Moore will confirm that I am right in saying this. All of the witnesses scheduled to come next are military witnesses, including military experts. These witnesses, as you were able to see with this witness, have a large number of various statements, records, evidence given in other trials. So all of this needs to be studied carefully and thoroughly. We have done a lot of it. What is important for us right now, more important than ever so far, are instructions from our clients precisely because of the profile of these witnesses. So far the witnesses that came here did not require us to constantly be in contact with our clients and receive instructions from them. But now, in view of the upcoming witnesses, we need to be in close contact with our clients, and it is because of that that I have concerns that this new schedule will be a hindrance in that sense. It will not facilitate us to have effective cross-examination. If we are only to contact our clients during the one-hour break, lunch break, and all of us need a break anyway, means that after we conclude trial at 4.30 in the afternoon, it will be impossible for us to go to the Detention Unit to see our clients and consult with them. We can be, under special circumstances, allowed to go to the detention unit after 4.30 in the afternoon, but you realise yourself just what a burden it would be for us to go there that late in order to consult them. So I wanted to inform you of this, as a Defence counsel, I feel it is my duty to inform you that such a new schedule, in view of the upcoming witnesses who are very technical, is going to be a significant burden for us. My instructions from my client were contrary to what I just told you, but I had to express the concern that I have that the nature of evidence that is scheduled for May is such that in view of the new schedule, it will be very difficult for us to consult our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to take this opportunity to add something to what my learned friend said. I think that his concern is identical to that of the team of Mr. Mrksic's defence. Especially when taking into account that the schedule is supposed to take place throughout May. This will be an extra effort for our clients, for everybody in the courtroom, including the Trial Chamber. However, in addition to what Mr. Lukic said, I think that there is another reason for concern with this new schedule. Namely the accused, after trial concludes at 4.30, will not arrive in the Detention Unit until 5.30 or perhaps even 6.00, given how busy it is at the Detention Unit, and how busy their schedule is. I was informed that the schedule for walk at the Detention Unit is such that the accused will be unable to have their walk for the next month because they will arrive at the Detention Unit too late. In addition to that, they will not have opportunity to exercise because once they arrive back at the Detention Unit they will have less than two hours, or perhaps just a bit more than two hours before they lock them up for the night in their cells. That probably would not have been a major concern if this new schedule were to be in place for just a week or so. But a whole month of this schedule will mean that our clients will have their rhythm disrupted, and that can affect their health. Because one month is quite a long period of time. Therefore, I fully support the submission given by Mr. Lukic and I am informing you about this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This is the first time that I fail to support my colleagues, whom I normally support in their submissions. I believe that my client has spent too long a time in Detention Unit, and therefore I would urge you to press on, to have the trial concluded as quickly as possible, so that all of these difficulties come to an end as soon as possible, the difficulties mentioned by my colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen. It needs to be appreciated that the Tribunal is normally forced to sit abnormal hours. That is, a morning session or an afternoon session. Starting earlier than a normal court in the morning, and finishing much later than a normal court in the afternoon because we have only three courtrooms and we need to have six trials running. And every week that goes by when we don't utilise that capacity means that not only does an existing trial run longer, but that other accused, most of whom are in custody, wait longer in custody before their trials can be heard. Therefore, whenever there is an opportunity to adjust to normal sitting hours, which happens occasionally in between other cases, we do so, so that we can, in fact, sit what would be a fairly normal court sitting day, which is an hour of hearing longer than we can fit in, if we're having two hearings a day. That way, effectively, getting six days into five days, and so shortening the length of the trial. And this has been the practice that has been followed by this Chamber in previous trials whenever the opportunity has arisen. We are always conscious of the need to obtain instructions from clients, but it would be somewhat surprising if it were not possible if some unexpected matter had arisen in the course of a day's evidence, that even a few minutes at the lunch break or a few minutes at the end of the day, or a few minutes the next morning here rather than at the detention centre, would not be sufficient to enable this new matter to be focused on and instructions obtained. You will see that next week, Wednesday afternoon has had to be freed because the Appeals Chamber needs to sit that day, so they need the courtroom in the afternoon. What we might do is to make some small adjustment to hours and to the timetable, and see whether the matter can proceed in practice with reasonably efficiency. And we're also conscious, of course, that not only are there concerns of the Defence, but the Prosecution must proof witnesses and so forth, and we are well aware of those matters. On Friday of next week what we might do, and here we're also conscious that there are those people not only in the courtroom but supporting the courtroom whose hours are governed by the time we sit who can be disadvantaged by an inability to travel. So we might, on the Friday, sit a normal morning, 9.00 in the morning to 1.45. That would next week leave you with Wednesday afternoon and Friday afternoon free, as on the ordinary programme. And if, unless something dramatic happens, we might achieve something like that in the weeks following by, say, starting later on the Monday, so that there is a morning freed up, finishing earlier on the Friday at the 1.45 time, so that there is an afternoon freed up, and see whether, by adjustments such as that, it proves more practical. It means we will not gain the full time advantage for which we had hoped, but it will nevertheless be a significant assistance in trying to ensure that this case finishes as soon as it properly can, which is in the interests of all people. So, with you reminded that on Wednesday of next week it will be a normal morning session, 0900 to 1.45, and with an adjustment to allow you to sit a normal morning session on the Friday, and with a Monday holiday, I would hope we will survive the ordeal of this major adjustment to life for the first week at least. And we will then see whether there can be life under this new ordeal. There are three judges who are affected by all of this as well, but somehow or other we have to manage. If that proves satisfactory, then we, the following week, would try the later start on the Monday and the 1.45 finish on the Friday, which will meet the concerns of another number of other people as well. And to see whether, by those means, it proves satisfactory. You will realise that this is a limited opportunity, shortly other cases will come on stream, and we will lose the opportunity to have the morning and afternoon use of the courtroom, and have to go back to having one or other, which will slow us down to a normal pace. So I hope those adjustments may prove sufficient, and I hope it will enable all the difficulties that have been raised to somehow or other be coped with. So we will adjourn now until 9.30 on Monday morning. I will get softer again. Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of May, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.54 p.m.,
